li.a: Monsoon Books: Escape by David McMillan
The Age: Cashed-up and bold as brass, he was the smart crim, but not as smart as the cops stalking him
The Sydney Morning Herald: There was a crooked man
BBC News: How to plan a successful jailbreak
London Evening Standard: Drug dealer who escaped Bangkok jail is on the run in London
News Shopper: Orpington drug smuggler David McMillan jailed for six years
MyLondon: I was put in chains in a Thai prison for smuggling drugs but escaped 2 weeks before my execution
The West Australian: From Caulfield Grammar to the Bangkok Hilton

content.p: David McMillan is a British-born, Australian-raised heroin trafficker who was convicted in Melbourne in 1983, arrested in Bangkok a decade later, and then did what no other Westerner is known to have done: he broke out of Klong Prem, a Bangkok prison his publisher calls Asia's most notorious, in August 1996. He was on a flight to Singapore within hours. He spent the following years in Pakistan, London and Scandinavia, was jailed again in Britain, and eventually turned his life into a string of books and a television drama.
Much of what is known about his methods and his escape comes from McMillan himself, and his own accounts do not always match the newspaper record. Where they differ, that is said below.
content.h2: From a television newsreader to the underworld
content.p: McMillan was born in Bayswater, London, the son of John McMillan, who after wartime service managed Rediffusion Television and later received a CBE. When David was about two, his mother, who had met an Italian film producer, was sent with him and his sister to Australia to have the producer's baby, and the producer, who vowed to send for them, never did, according to The Sydney Morning Herald. He grew up in Melbourne with a succession of stepfathers. At 12 he presented a children's news programme on the Nine Network, which his publisher says came after an earlier first arrest at 10, for breaking into a match factory.

School did not hold him. The Age says he was expelled from Caulfield Grammar after trying to make LSD in the school laboratory. The Sydney Morning Herald says he vanished at the end of year 11 after he was caught forging prescriptions and cheques. Either way he drifted into work as a film projectionist at a seedy city cinema, where he met people selling drugs. His own telling, quoted by the Sydney Morning Herald, is that his first serious smuggling was hashish carried from India inside a radio, and that a customs officer who smelled it simply let him go.

From there, the Sydney Morning Herald reports, he moved on to heroin, using several passports and a friendly travel agent, first alone and then with Michael Sullivan. He said he made enormous sums, never enough to make him stop. The Age says that by the time he came to police attention he had nine identities and safe houses in Melbourne, Bangkok, London, Hong Kong and Brussels, and had made 11 overseas trips in a single year. Police found a list of 43 women he used as couriers, 38 birth certificates and 27 passports in false names. His publisher credits his group with developing the bag-swap system at Sydney's Kingsford-Smith airport.

Victoria's Bureau of Criminal Intelligence concluded that the syndicate was too large for one force. The result was Operation Aries, a task force of Victorian detectives, Australian Federal Police and customs officers, which The Age calls the template for later investigations of sophisticated drug syndicates. McMillan, codenamed "M", was its main target. He said he was warned that a task force was being formed and kept going anyway. He knew his telephones were being tapped.

On 5 December 1981 he met Chowdury, a Thai associate who police said was carrying two cutlery boxes of heroin. A watching officer called in an arrest team, but his radio message went unanswered because he was standing in a dead spot, and the suspects got away. McMillan later boasted that he had picked the place for that reason. Police told The Age it was luck, not planning.

In January 1982 Aries arrested McMillan, his partner Clelia Vigano, Sullivan, Sullivan's girlfriend Mary Escolar Castillo, Chowdury and others. Vigano was the daughter of a well-known Melbourne restaurant family. About a month later she and Castillo died in what The Age describes as a deliberately lit fire at Fairlea Women's Prison. MyLondon, in a 2021 interview, dates the fire to 1981 and calls Vigano McMillan's first wife; the other sources place the arrests in January 1982 and describe her as his partner. The Sydney Morning Herald says that, by McMillan's own account, his sorrow over her death was the one remorse he did not fake.
content.h2: The trial and the helicopter plan
content.p: Before the trial, a plan was hatched to get McMillan, Sullivan and Chowdury out of Pentridge Prison by helicopter. As The Age tells it, the helicopter was to land inside the walls, a make-up artist was to disguise the three men, and they were to fly out of the country, with an ocean-going yacht as a second option. The Sydney Morning Herald says a tip to police foiled it. A former British soldier was convicted over the conspiracy. The Evening Standard reports that McMillan paid £250,000 toward the attempt.

The prosecution became Victoria's first super-trial. The Age reports that it ran for 100 days, with 175 witnesses and an 8,000-page transcript, and that the jury deliberated for a record eight days. The Sydney Morning Herald says the prosecution case was that McMillan was a trafficker, while his defence was that he was a user who paid for his habit by smuggling gold and gems. The jury acquitted all three men on every charge but one: conspiracy to import heroin. For that, the Sydney Morning Herald says, the judge sentenced them to 17 years each, designed to send a message to educated young people who should have known better. The Age gives the sentence as 15 years. McMillan was 26 when he went in and 37 when he was released, according to The Age, and he was paroled in 1993.

Police surveillance resumed almost as soon as he was out, and by his own account he went straight back to his old methods. The Sydney Morning Herald says a former jailmate tipped off police, and that a retired officer told The Age that Australian police let him go to Thailand because they thought he might be hanged. In late 1993 Thai police arrested him. Accounts of the arrest differ. McMillan told the BBC that four policemen walked into a travel agency in Chinatown and took him. MyLondon reports his later version, in which he was stopped at the airport with two passports in different names and the police then found 40 grams of heroin that had been thrown away. He denied it was his. He was travelling under the alias Daniel Westlake and, according to him, was in Thailand to collect money earned before his Australian arrest, which he was not allowed to leave Australia for while on parole. The Sydney Morning Herald says that on the charge he faced, the best he could hope for was a death sentence commuted to 99 years.

He was taken to Klong Prem, which he told BBC World Service held about 12,000 prisoners. MyLondon records his claim of cells built for 56 that held up to 130, and of beatings of those who tried to escape. His wealth, the Standard says, bought him a cook, servants and a sanitary toilet; he told the BBC he first secured what he called a private cell.

McMillan says he began planning on the day of his arrest and drew up some 15 schemes in two years. He told the BBC he chose building six because its window bars were the thinnest, and that only five earlier escape attempts were remembered, none successful. When his lawyer warned him that a death sentence would come within two weeks, he moved. The account below is his own, with the Sydney Morning Herald's and the Evening Standard's versions as cross-checks.

One night in August 1996, using hacksaw blades smuggled into the prison, he and a cellmate worked at a window bar until it could be bent. McMillan squeezed through and lowered himself to the ground on a rope. He then collected picture frames from a prison workshop and long bamboo poles from a factory and, by his account, built ladders to cross the inner walls, a sewage-filled ditch and the outer wall with its electrified wire. By dawn he was outside. His final trick, which the Sydney Morning Herald and the Standard both report, was to walk off under an open umbrella, on the theory that escaping prisoners do not carry one.

He picked up a doctored passport and was at the airport by morning. The Sydney Morning Herald says he was on a flight to Singapore by 10.20 a.m., boarding as guards arrived to look for him. MyLondon says he spent his last $500 on the ticket, under the name Charles McLintock. Months later, the Sydney Morning Herald says, Robert McClelland, later Australia's attorney-general, said in a speech that the prisoner had escaped in "exceptional and athletic circumstances", and that he had left the Australian embassy a note thanking staff for their work.

The Sydney Morning Herald says McMillan reached London after hiding with powerful friends in a remote province of Pakistan. His publisher says that from the Afghan border he returned to the smuggler's trail and says he escaped a life sentence in Pakistan and any serious sentence in Colombia, until a term in Scandinavia ended that life. MyLondon quotes him as saying that less than two years after the escape he was beaten and given electric shocks by police in Pakistan, who suspected him of involvement in smuggling 14 kilograms of opium, until a British embassy official heard of an "English foreigner" being held and stopped it. These are McMillan's claims; no official record of them was among the pages consulted. In 2009 the Sydney Morning Herald met him in a house in Chislehurst, south of London, where he lived with a partner he said he met while she was visiting her husband in a prison in Pakistan.

The Evening Standard says he was arrested at Heathrow in 2003 carrying half a kilogram of heroin, and received a four-year sentence, and that he was then out on parole. In the 2012 interview he said he was going straight. In March 2012, according to the News Shopper, Border Force officers seized a parcel travelling from Pakistan to Orpington; inside two shirts were 35 grams of heroin sewn into the collars. Bromley police arrested McMillan after he took delivery, and found small packets of heroin, scales and cutting agents at his home. At 56 he was jailed for six years at Croydon Crown Court for trafficking Class A drugs and possessing heroin with intent to supply.
content.h2: Books, a drama and an extradition fight
content.p: McMillan's first book, Escape, was on sale in Asia by 2012 according to the Evening Standard; News Shopper dates his memoirs to 2007, while the Sydney Morning Herald in September 2009 called the book just released in Australia. Critics quoted by his publisher compared it with a thriller. His second book, McVillain, The Man Who Got Away, was published in 2011, according to The Age. A third, Unforgiving Destiny, is named by MyLondon. The Nine Network's The Underbelly Files: The Man Who Got Away, with Toby Schmitz as McMillan and Claire van der Boom as Vigano, was shown in 2011.

In 2014 Thailand asked Britain to extradite him on the 1993 heroin charge, for which he was never convicted. His publisher says the Thai government withdrew its request after almost two years of hearings, one week before he was due to be taken to Bangkok. MyLondon says he spent two years in Wandsworth Prison between 2014 and 2016 and that he now fits CCTV cameras for a living. McMillan has said that Thailand did not really want him, and that he accepted its explanation when he pointed out the warrants were more than 20 years old.
